clue.text: It shows if a cadet loses it

indicators.note: the phrase 'if a cadet' sheds its first and last letters, leaving the answer inside it

explanation.surface: A remark that something becomes visible when a young officer trainee mislays it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'loses it' drops the I at the front and the T at the back of IFACADET. 'It shows' is the definition: the front of a building, or a false front, is the part on display.
explanation.definitionFit: A building's front face, or a person's outward show, is the part that is visible to onlookers.

clue.text: Infer cash is unusual in business arrangement

indicators.note: the letters of 'Infer cash' are put in an unusual order, so they are rearranged

explanation.surface: Someone concludes that money is out of the ordinary in a commercial deal.
explanation.walkthrough: 'is unusual' rearranges INFERCASH.
explanation.definitionFit: A licence to trade under a parent company's brand, such as a fast-food outlet, is a commercial deal.

clue.text: Given supernatural protection, but many get hurt

parts.note: C is the Roman numeral for a hundred, so many
harmed means hurt

explanation.surface: Someone shielded by magic, though plenty of others are injured.
explanation.walkthrough: C (100 in Roman numerals) stands for 'many', a common crossword convention.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who leads a charmed life is protected as if by a spell or magic.

clue.text: Fail in search for a sound-only cartridge

explanation.surface: Someone fails to find what they want, as if firing a dud round.
explanation.walkthrough: The second reading takes the phrase literally: to pull out a blank, a cartridge that makes a bang but has no bullet.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom means to come up empty-handed; literally, to pull out a blank round, which only makes a noise.

clue.text: A pyrotechnic stone…

explanation.surface: The first half of a two-part riddle about a firework and a gem.
explanation.walkthrough: The ellipsis runs on into 10 across, which supplies another kind of stone.
explanation.definitionFit: A hand-held firework that throws off sparks; also slang for a diamond, a gem that glitters.

clue.text: Staff of newspaper in Shanghai?

parts.note: the press is the newspaper world
a gang is a body of workers, a staff

explanation.surface: Asks about the employees of a paper based in the Chinese city.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Shanghai' looks like the place; it is the verb meaning to kidnap a man into a ship's crew. The question mark flags the trick.
explanation.definitionFit: To force someone into service against their will, as sailors once were, is to coerce them into joining.

clue.text: By the sound of it, moved boat in anchorage

indicators.note: the clue says the word is judged by how it is pronounced, so a word said aloud is spelt another way

parts.note: to move a boat with oars is to row it, so rowed

explanation.surface: A craft paddled into a sheltered mooring.
explanation.walkthrough: A roads (or roadstead) is a sheltered stretch of water where ships can ride at anchor.
explanation.definitionFit: Roads, or a roadstead, are sheltered waters off shore where ships lie at anchor.

clue.text: Grill-room in the French style

indicators.note: the room sits inside the French article, so one piece goes within the other

parts.note: le is French for 'the'
an attic is a room under the roof

explanation.surface: A grill restaurant decorated in Gallic fashion.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Grill-room' looks like one word, but 'Grill' alone is the definition, as in a grille; 'style' only dresses the surface.
explanation.definitionFit: A grille is a framework of crossed strips, an open criss-cross screen.

clue.text: Unstable boxer

explanation.surface: A wobbly fighter in the ring.
explanation.definitionFit: Shaky and wobbly; also a famous boxer, Marciano, or the film fighter Balboa.

clue.text: Make trouble in prison

explanation.surface: Someone causes a disturbance behind bars.
explanation.definitionFit: To agitate or stir things up; and slang for jail.

clue.text: … and an immovable one

parts.note: continuing 4 across, 'one' is a stone: a legendary stone so hard nothing can shift it, whose name also means unyielding

explanation.surface: The second half of the riddle: after the firework and glittering gem, a stone that will not budge.
explanation.definitionFit: The old name for a mythical unbreakable stone, which also serves as an adjective for someone who refuses to change their mind.

clue.text: With spring, I visit ruined castle

indicators.note: to visit is to go into a place, so the letter I goes inside the other letters
a ruined castle is broken down, so its letters are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A bouncy tourist announces they are off to see a castle in ruins.
explanation.walkthrough: 'ruined' rearranges CASTLE into ELASTC, and 'visit' puts I inside it.
explanation.definitionFit: Something with spring stretches and bounces back to its shape, like a rubber band.

clue.text: Meet to hand over money

explanation.surface: An instruction for a rendezvous at which cash will be paid over.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase means to encounter someone by chance, and, informally, to pay up what is owed.

clue.text: Financial centre — that's only half the truth

indicators.note: only half of the word for truth is used, here its second four letters

parts.note: veracity means truthfulness, the truth

explanation.surface: A cynical remark that a banking district is not to be wholly trusted.
explanation.walkthrough: VERACITY has eight letters; 'only half' keeps its back half. The City is London's financial district.
explanation.definitionFit: The City of London is the UK's banking and finance quarter, so a financial centre is a city.

clue.text: Sat, and then did the twist here

indicators.note: the twist is a dance, and doing it means twisting, so the letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: Someone sat down, then got up and danced the twist at this venue.
explanation.walkthrough: 'did the twist' rearranges SATANDTHEN. 'here' points to the place the whole sentence describes: a tea dance (French thé dansant), where one might sit and then dance.
explanation.definitionFit: A tea dance is an afternoon gathering where people take tea and dance, the place the clue describes.

clue.text: Take a drink, eluding getting drunk

indicators.note: someone getting drunk staggers about, so the letters of 'eluding' are scrambled

explanation.surface: Someone has a drink while managing to avoid getting drunk.
explanation.walkthrough: 'getting drunk' rearranges ELUDING.
explanation.definitionFit: To indulge, informally, is to have an alcoholic drink, giving in to a pleasure.

clue.text: Remaining fresh, like you said

explanation.surface: Someone agrees, saying a thing still seems new, just as was claimed.
explanation.walkthrough: The second definition is heard: 'like you said' sounds like 'like yew, said' — the yew tree keeps its leaves all year.
explanation.definitionFit: Plants that keep their leaves all year stay green; the yew is such a tree, so 'like yew' describes it.

clue.text: Bring to a successful conclusion an exotic letter to a lady

parts.note: 'an' gives the single letter A
chi is a letter of the Greek alphabet, foreign to English
Eve is a woman's name, the first lady

explanation.surface: Someone completes a task by sending a foreign letter to a woman.
explanation.walkthrough: CHI is the Greek letter written X; EVE is the biblical first woman.
explanation.definitionFit: To bring something off successfully is to accomplish it, reach the goal.

clue.text: "Always" — coda takes artist about two seconds

parts.note: a coda is the closing passage of a piece of music, its end

indicators.note: the painter's name goes round the other letters, so they sit inside it

parts.note: Sir Peter Lely was a 17th-century portrait painter
s is the abbreviation for second, so two of them

explanation.surface: A piece's closing section takes a painter around two seconds to finish.
explanation.walkthrough: Sir Peter Lely, painter at Charles II's court, is a stock crossword artist; 'about' wraps his name round the two S abbreviations. 'coda' is musical: a closing passage.
explanation.definitionFit: Without ever stopping or finishing, continually and forever.

clue.text: Space for vessels in the river

indicators.note: the vessels sit inside the river, so one word goes inside the other

parts.note: the Exe is a river in Devon, a crossword favourite
pans are cooking vessels

explanation.surface: Room for boats on a river.
explanation.walkthrough: 'vessels' tempts you towards boats; here they are kitchen pans. The Exe is a river in south-west England.
explanation.definitionFit: A wide open stretch of land, sea or sky is a broad area of space.

clue.text: Acclaim from archbishop in hell

indicators.note: the archbishop is placed inside hell, so one piece goes within the other

parts.note: the pit is a name for hell
William Laud was an Archbishop of Canterbury under Charles I

explanation.surface: Praise coming from a churchman in the underworld.
explanation.walkthrough: William Laud, Archbishop of Canterbury under Charles I, is a stock crossword archbishop; 'in' places him within the pit, an old name for hell.
explanation.definitionFit: Praise or applause given to someone is a round of acclaim.

clue.text: An unexpected event makes theatre-goers object

parts.note: the gods are the highest gallery in a theatre and, by extension, its occupants
an end is an aim or object

explanation.surface: A surprise happens when theatre audiences raise a protest.
explanation.walkthrough: 'object' reads as a verb (protest) but is the noun meaning goal. In British theatres, 'the gods' are the cheap seats in the top gallery.
explanation.definitionFit: A godsend is a welcome stroke of luck arriving out of the blue.

clue.text: Censor one performing an impression

parts.note: to censor a text is to edit it
I is the Roman numeral one
an actor performing is on stage, so on

explanation.surface: A censor watches an impressionist do their act.
explanation.walkthrough: 'impression' suggests mimicry, but it means a print run of a book.
explanation.definitionFit: A print run of a book, all copies made at one time, is an issue or printing.

clue.text: Hit friends about

indicators.note: about here means turned round, so the word for friends is read backwards

parts.note: pals are friends

explanation.surface: A punch thrown among companions.
explanation.walkthrough: 'about' turns PALS round.
explanation.definitionFit: A smack with the open hand is a blow, a strike.

clue.text: Clean up gambling

explanation.surface: A gambler cleans out the betting.
explanation.definitionFit: To brush a floor clean; also a sweepstake, a betting pool.

clue.text: A horse galloped outside to get more power

annotationWithheld.why: A horse galloped outside to get more power (10), printed so on the scan: A + GG + RAN gives AGGRAN, but no reading of 'outside to get' supplies DISE, so the wordplay cannot be completed honestly
annotationWithheld.clue: A horse galloped outside to get more power

clue.text: Scoff in the bar

explanation.surface: Someone sneers in the pub.
explanation.definitionFit: To rail is to complain bitterly or jeer; a rail is also a rod or bar.

clue.text: Spoken of rather a lot in the early stages

indicators.note: the starts of the words are all that is wanted, so each word gives its first letter

explanation.surface: A remark about how something was much discussed at the beginning.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in the early stages' takes the first letters of 'of rather a lot'.
explanation.definitionFit: Spoken words are said by mouth rather than written down.

clue.text: Red ones move back

indicators.note: the letters of 'Red ones' are shifted about, so they are rearranged

explanation.surface: Communists are told to retreat.
explanation.walkthrough: 'move back' reads as one phrase, but 'move' is the anagram signal and 'back' alone is the definition, as a verb meaning support.
explanation.definitionFit: To back a candidate or cheque is to support or sign it, giving approval.

clue.text: Miss Liddell not completely absorbed in its characters

indicators.note: one piece is soaked up inside another, so it goes within the letters of 'its'

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: the name is not given whole, so its last letter is dropped

parts.note: Alice Liddell was the girl who inspired Lewis Carroll's Alice books

explanation.surface: The young Alice Liddell, only partly engrossed in the people of a story.
explanation.walkthrough: 'not completely' drops the final E of Alice, and 'absorbed in' puts what is left inside 'its'. 'characters' suggests people in a book but means printed letters, here sloping type.
explanation.definitionFit: Italic type is a style of sloping printed letters, so these are typographic characters.

clue.text: Piano — instrument rejected by worker in a huff

parts.note: p is the musical abbreviation for piano, softly

indicators.note: rejected means thrown back, so the instrument's name is read backwards

parts.note: a lute is a stringed instrument
an ant is the classic worker insect

explanation.surface: A labourer sulks after a piano and another instrument are turned down.
explanation.walkthrough: 'rejected' turns the lute round so it reads backwards between the piano sign and the ant. 'worker' is a stock crossword clue for an ant or bee.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone sulky and peevish is in a sulk, a bad temper.

clue.text: Unwilling to give smart-money ultimately

parts.note: to smart is to sting, as a cut does

indicators.note: ultimately means at the end, so only the last letter of 'money' is used

explanation.surface: A clever financier, in the end, refuses to hand any over.
explanation.walkthrough: 'smart-money' looks like one phrase but splits: 'smart' (to hurt) gives STING, and Y is the last letter of 'money'.
explanation.definitionFit: A mean, tight-fisted person is reluctant to part with cash.
